summary: SpaceX's Starship rapid reusability enables orbital compute and Starlink Direct-to-Cell, representing transformative value creation
summary_extended: Baker argues that SpaceX's Starship rocket — which now controls approximately 85% of global mass-to-orbit capacity — is the critical enabling technology for two transformative near-term opportunities: orbital compute satellites and Starlink Direct-to-Cell connectivity. He bases this conviction on direct conversations with SpaceX engineers at Starbase, who confirmed that the primary remaining technical risk for orbital compute was Starship reusability (including catching the upper stage), a challenge now being actively demonstrated. Baker cites Brad Gerstner's projection that the first orbital compute satellites could launch as early as 2027, contingent on continued Starship reusability progress. The investment implication centers on SpaceX itself as the dominant beneficiary, though SpaceX is privately held and not directly investable via US-listed equities. No US-listed public equity is an unambiguous direct subject or direct beneficiary of this specific thesis without speculative inference.
detail: Baker states SpaceX controls 85% of mass to orbit. Rapid reusability of Starship (including catching the upper stage) is the key enabling technology for: (1) orbital compute satellites (first launch targeted 2027 per Brad Gerstner); (2) Starlink Direct-to-Cell. SpaceX engineers have solved cooling and design challenges for orbital compute satellites — their remaining concern is Starship reusability, which is now being addressed.
confidence_evidence: Baker has spent significant time at Starbase, spoke directly with SpaceX engineers, and frames orbital compute as a near-certain outcome contingent on Starship reusability progress now being demonstrated.
